passage: Afreen began taking the longer lane past the flour mill so she would not pass Jagdish at the tea stall. She told her cousins she did not care. But every day she slowed down at the spot where they used to share roasted peanuts, and on the local bus her hand kept going to the empty seat beside her. One evening she sat on the terrace and said quietly to the darkening sky, "I miss him. I miss how we were." Saying it made her chest hurt a little less. The next day she told her aunt, "I lost my best friend," and her aunt sat down beside her and made tea. Afreen did not call Jagdish. But she stopped pretending.

qa.q: Which way did Afreen take after the betrayal?
qa.a: She took the longer lane past the flour mill.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she slowed down at the peanut spot, though she told her cousins she did not care?
qa.a: She was grieving the friendship; she pretended not to care, but slowing down and reaching for the empty seat show how much she missed him.

qa.q: How did naming her loss help Afreen?
qa.a: Saying it aloud made her chest hurt less and let her aunt sit with her, so she did not carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Afreen's aunt see her that day?
qa.a: As someone who was hurting and needed company more than advice, since she sat down beside Afreen and made tea.

grounding: A teen mourns the loss of a friendship after a betrayal; naming the grief helps instead of pretending not to care.

passage: Jeevan's history essay came back with the lowest mark he had ever got and a comment that the argument was missing. He was sure he had written one. He did not complain to the class, and he did not sit in silence either. That evening he underlined the paragraph, copied the marking rubric from the school portal and waited by Ms Rashmi's table after class. "Ma'am, may I show you where I think my argument is? I might have misread what the rubric wants." She read the paragraph twice. "Ah. Page three was stuck to page four. I only read half your essay." She corrected the mark and said, "Thank you for asking politely rather than telling me off." Jeevan felt his shoulders drop.

qa.q: What did Jeevan bring to show Ms Rashmi?
qa.a: He brought the underlined paragraph and the marking rubric.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan say he might have misread what the rubric wants?
qa.a: He wanted to raise his concern politely without accusing her, and left room for the possibility that he was the one who was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do if the teacher had disagreed?
qa.a: He could listen to her reasons, ask how to improve, or take the concern to the coordinator or head through the school's proper channel.

qa.q: How might Ms Rashmi have felt when Jeevan approached her?
qa.a: She was probably relieved that he asked calmly, since she admitted her mistake and thanked him.

grounding: A student raises a concern about marking politely with evidence instead of staying silent or being disrespectful.

passage:
Thursday, late.

Had a fight at lunch today. My friend said Santosh was rude to that reporter in the clip, and that his last film was boring. I said the reporter must have deserved it and the film was a masterpiece, and I didn't speak to my friend for the whole break. Everything Santosh does is right, I told myself.

But at home I watched the clip again, and he really did snap at her for no reason. Something in my stomach turned. I felt like a traitor for even thinking it. Maybe I can love his songs and still think that was wrong. Maybe he's a person and not a god. I'll say sorry to my friend tomorrow.

- Lalit

qa.q: What did Lalit say about the reporter at lunch?
qa.a: He said the reporter must have deserved it.

qa.q: Why did Lalit feel like a traitor when he watched the clip again?
qa.a: Lalit had always defended Santosh, so seeing that Santosh snapped for no reason felt like disloyalty, even though Lalit could see it was wrong.

qa.q: How can Lalit keep admiring Santosh's songs in a healthy way?
qa.a: Lalit can enjoy the songs while allowing disagreement, and remember that Santosh is a person who can be wrong.

qa.q: How might Lalit's friend have felt at lunch?
qa.a: The friend was probably annoyed or hurt at being ignored for the whole break, having only shared a fair point.

grounding: A teen treats an idol as flawless and defends every act, then starts to see the idol as human.

passage: Note from Sonali, school counsellor. Mehak came to see me on Monday after reading that the author she admired most had been found to have copied parts of another writer's book. She said, "Everything I believed is fake," and told me she had torn her poster off the wall that morning. She was shaking a little. I did not tell her to stop being upset. I asked which ideas of the author she still thought were true, and she named the essays on patience and starting again. We talked about how ideas can stand on their own even when a person disappoints us. By Thursday the poster was in a drawer, but the book was back on her desk.

qa.q: Where did the poster end up by Thursday?
qa.a: The poster was in a drawer, and the book was back on her desk.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she said everything she believed was fake?
qa.a: She felt crushed and let down, since her admiration for the author had felt like part of what she believed.

qa.q: How could Mehak keep what is good in the author's ideas?
qa.a: She can judge each essay on its own merits, keep the ones that still make sense, and admire people without expecting them to be perfect.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Mehak's reaction?
qa.a: As a normal part of growing up, since the disappointment shows how much Mehak cared, and Sonali guided Mehak instead of dismissing it.

grounding: A teen is crushed when an admired author turns out to be flawed and learns to keep the ideas but drop the idolisation.

passage: Only one place was left on the relay squad, and it would go to Sofia or Layla. Every morning at six, Sofia found Layla already swimming laps in the pool in Marseille. At first the sight made her stomach twist. Then Sofia began to time herself against Layla's lap splits and asked the coach to check her turns. One evening a teammate joked about hiding Layla's goggles before the trials. Sofia said, "No. If I win the place, I want it to be mine." When the results came, Layla got it by a small margin. Sofia shook her hand, still out of breath, and said, "Your turns are unreal. Show me sometime?" Layla laughed and said yes.

qa.q: What did a teammate joke about hiding?
qa.a: The teammate joked about hiding Layla's goggles.

qa.q: Why did Sofia refuse to hide Layla's goggles?
qa.a: She wanted any win to be her own, and she used Layla as a benchmark to improve rather than as an enemy to beat by tricks. 😊

qa.q: What could Sofia do after losing the place?
qa.a: She could keep working on her turns, ask Layla and the coach for tips, and aim for the next selection.

qa.q: How might Layla have felt when Sofia shook her hand?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and relieved by the respect, and glad the rivalry stayed friendly.

grounding: A rival is treated as a benchmark: training harder without sabotage or rumours.

passage:
Rashmi: you awake?
Yash: its 2:14am. yes
Rashmi: i keep refreshing her mock test score. shes 3 marks ahead 😔
Yash: for the quiz team place?
Rashmi: yes. i cant sleep. i cant think about anything except beating her
Rashmi: i studied 1 hour today. i spent 3 checking her
Yash: thats not studying rash
Rashmi: i hate her
Yash: i think you hate being behind. not the same thing. what would you do if you had nobody to watch?
Rashmi: finish the chemistry chapters
Yash: do that. sleep first 😴
Rashmi: ok. sorry for waking you
Yash: text me tomorrow

qa.q: What time was it when Rashmi messaged Yash?
qa.a: It was 2:14am.

qa.q: What is Rashmi feeling about the other girl, and how does it affect her studying?
qa.a: Rashmi feels hatred and can't stop fixating on beating the other girl; Rashmi spent 3 hours checking scores and only 1 hour studying.

qa.q: What would help Rashmi tonight and tomorrow?
qa.a: Rashmi could sleep first and then spend the time on the chemistry chapters instead of checking the other girl's scores.

qa.q: How does Yash see Rashmi's message?
qa.a: Yash sees a tired friend who is stuck watching someone else, and tells Rashmi that hate may really be about being behind.

grounding: A teen fixates on defeating a rival, losing sleep and study time, and recognises the obsession drains energy from her own growth.

passage:
Group chat, 10:40 pm
A: did u see Darshan's voice note
B: he sounded like a frog
C: send it to the other section
A: hes such a clown
B: everyone screenshot it

Urmila typed "stop" and deleted it. Typed "this isn't funny" and deleted that too.

Private message
Urmila: hey. i saw the chat. its not ok
Urmila: do you want to talk?
Darshan: i left the group
Urmila: good. i'm here. i can come with you to tell our class teacher tomorrow if you want
Darshan: ok
Darshan: thanks for messaging me

qa.q: What did Urmila write privately to Darshan?
qa.a: She wrote "i saw the chat. its not ok" and asked, "do you want to talk?"

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling when she typed and deleted her messages in the group chat?
qa.a: Urmila seemed uneasy and unsure; typing and deleting twice suggests a wish to speak up, perhaps held back by fear of the group turning on Urmila.

qa.q: What options did Urmila have, and which did she choose?
qa.a: Urmila could join in, stay silent or defend Darshan publicly; Urmila chose to message Darshan privately and offered to go to the teacher with him.

qa.q: How might Darshan have felt when he saw Urmila's message?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved not to be alone after being laughed at, and his short replies show how much it mattered.

grounding: A teen sees a pile-on against one classmate and, rather than join or stay silent, messages the target privately.

passage:
"Give me my phone," hissed Parveen. "That stranger called my drawing garbage. I'm writing something back that will make him cry."

"Wait." Her older brother Ujjwal held out his hand. "Show me what you wrote."

She showed him the draft.

"That's savage. Which is exactly what he wants, right? Something to screenshot."

"So I just let him win?"

"What happens if you don't answer?"

"He gets bored, maybe."

"Mute him. Sleep. Look at it in the morning."

Parveen sighed, muted the account and put her phone on the shelf. The next morning she read her draft once and wrinkled her nose. "Glad that never went out."

qa.q: What did the stranger call Parveen's drawing?
qa.a: He called it garbage.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about the stranger's comment, and what did she want to do?
qa.a: She felt angry and insulted, and she wanted to make him cry with a sharp reply.

qa.q: What steps helped Parveen in the end?
qa.a: She did not reply, muted the account, went to sleep and read her draft again in the morning.

qa.q: Why might the stranger want a reply from Parveen?
qa.a: Ujjwal points out he is likely after something to screenshot, so an angry reply would give him exactly what he wants.

grounding: An online stranger baits a teen into a heated reply; she learns to mute, not feed the troll, and sleep before answering.

passage: Every evening Aiko's family lit incense at the small altar in their Osaka flat, and Aiko copied the bows. Lately she had been asking herself why prayers were answered for some people and not for others, and whether she truly believed or just went along. She felt guilty for even wondering, as if she was letting her grandparents down. At last she asked her friend Yuki, who went to a temple with his own family, whether he ever had questions. "All the time," said Yuki. "My mother says questions are part of how it grows." The next Sunday Aiko asked her grandmother, in a small voice, why they prayed. Her grandmother did not look angry. She said she had asked the same thing as a girl, and she would share what she had found.

qa.q: Where did Aiko's family light incense?
qa.a: They lit incense at the small altar in their Osaka flat.

qa.q: Why did Aiko feel guilty for wondering?
qa.a: She felt as if asking questions was letting her grandparents down.

qa.q: How could Aiko keep exploring her questions?
qa.a: She can keep asking trusted people like her grandmother and Yuki and think things through; honest questioning can lead to deeper faith or to a reasoned change.

qa.q: How might Aiko's grandmother have felt about the question?
qa.a: She did not look angry, and saying she had asked the same thing as a girl suggests she understood and welcomed it.

grounding: A teen doubts religion and feels guilty, then finds that questions are a normal part of building conviction.

passage: I'm Devika. Since last year I sit for ten minutes of quiet meditation each morning, and on Sundays I help Manjula Aunty serve khichdi at the temple community kitchen. It steadies me. For the first few months I also got proud. I looked down on classmates who never prayed, and once I even told one of them so. Manjula Aunty heard it and said quietly, "Seva that makes you feel bigger isn't seva." It stung. I went home and thought about it for days. Now I try to serve without keeping score. Last week a classmate who doesn't believe carried the water pots with me, and we ended up laughing so hard we spilled half of them.

qa.q: What does Devika help serve at the temple community kitchen?
qa.a: She helps serve khichdi.

qa.q: What did Devika feel when Manjula Aunty said seva that makes you feel bigger isn't seva?
qa.a: It stung, but Devika thought about it for days and realised the pride was making Devika look down on others.

qa.q: What has Devika changed since then?
qa.a: Devika now serves without keeping score and treats classmates who don't pray with warmth instead of contempt. 🙂

qa.q: How might the classmate Devika once told off have felt?
qa.a: They were probably hurt or judged, since Devika looked down on them for not praying.

grounding: A teen deepens devotion through meditation and service and learns devotion should make her kinder, not contemptuous of others.
